items.prose: An interviewer sets a ledger and then follows up. A desk trades one symbol. It buys 8 at £60, sells 3 at £64, buys 15 at £52 and sells 10 at £58.

parts.question: What is the realised profit by average cost, in £?

widget.accept: 52: 12 from the first sale and 40 from the second

feedback.generic: Not quite right. After the second buy the average is £54.

byKey.fifo: That is the FIFO profit. Average cost uses £54 for the second sale.
byKey.second: You counted only the second sale. The first sale realised £12.

explain.text: The first sale realises $3 \times (64 - 60) = 12$. The buy of 15 at £52 brings 20 shares to an average of $(5 \times 60 + 15 \times 52) / 20 = 54$. The second sale realises $10 \times (58 - 54) = 40$.

parts.question: What is the realised profit by FIFO, in £?

widget.accept: 32: 12 on the first sale, -10 and +30 on the second

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The second sale uses the five shares left at £60, then five at £52.

byKey.avg: That is the average-cost profit. FIFO uses each lot's own price.
byKey.skip: You left out the loss on the five £60 shares. They sell first, at £58.

explain.text: The first sale uses the £60 lot and realises $3 \times 4 = 12$. The second takes 5 shares at £60, realising $5 \times (58 - 60) = -10$, then 5 at £52, realising $5 \times 6 = 30$. The total is 32.

parts.question: How much more is the average-cost profit than the FIFO profit, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the FIFO profit from the average-cost profit.

byKey.flip: You subtracted the other way. The average-cost profit is the larger.
byKey.sum: You added the two profits. The question asks for the difference.

explain.text: Average cost realises 52 and FIFO realises 32, so the gap is 20. The methods split the same cash gain differently between sales. Total profit once all shares are sold is the same.

items.prose: As `LRUCache`, but when full drop the entry used the fewest times. Ties go to the least recently used of those. A get or put of an existing key counts as a use. A new key starts with one use. Capacity 0 stores nothing.
items.question: Write `LFUCache(capacity)` with `get(key)` and `put(key, value)`, both in constant time.

tests.setup: ops = [[0, i, i] for i in range(50000)] + [[1, i] for i in range(49000, 50000)]

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests: capacity 0, a counted update, ties, frequency over recency and 50,000 puts.

feedback.correct: Buckets of keys by use count, and the lowest count tracked.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: the put of 17 evicts key 16, used once. The put of 18 evicts key 15, the older of two keys used twice.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 has capacity 0. Nothing is stored.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 ties on one use each. The least recently used goes first.
byKey.test-4: Test 4: key 6 has one use, key 5 has three. The put of 7 evicts key 6.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 mixes counts of 1 and 2 on a full cache of 3.
byKey.test-6: Test 6: a put of a stored key updates it and counts as a use.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has 50,000 puts. Every call must be constant time.
byKey.test-8: Test 8: key 1 has two uses, key 2 has one. The put of 3 evicts key 2, though key 1 is older.
byKey.test-9: Test 9: the second put of key 1 is a use. Key 1 has two uses, so the put of 3 evicts key 2.

explain.text: Keep a dict of values and a dict of counts. Each count has an ordered dict of keys, oldest use first, and the lowest count is tracked. A touch moves a key up a bucket, and the victim is the first key of the lowest one.

items.prose: `hit(t)` records a hit at whole second `t`. `count(t)` returns the hits at times greater than `t - 300` and at most `t`. Calls come in non-decreasing time.
items.question: Write `HitCounter` with `hit(t)` and `count(t)`, using a fixed amount of memory.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. They cover window edges, an empty counter, repeated times, times that are 299 mod 300 and 50,000 hits.

feedback.correct: A ring of 300 slots, each stamped with its second.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 slides the window: the hits at 1, 2 and 3 leave at 301, 302 and 303.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 counts on an empty counter. Return 0.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has two hits in one second, then the window moves past them.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 reuses a slot: the hits at 5 and 305 share index 5.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has 50,000 hits. A list of every hit is the slow, large answer.

explain.text: Slot `t % 300` holds the second it was last used for and its count. A hit in a new second resets the slot. A count adds the slots whose second lies in $(t - 300, t]$.

items.question: Say aloud how you would design a per-client rate limit for an exchange gateway.

widget.prompt: Say this aloud, timing yourself to three minutes, then write the main points. Design a per-client rate limit for an exchange gateway. Compare a fixed window, a sliding log and a token bucket on accuracy, memory and bursts. Use a limit of 100 a minute, with 100 requests at second 59 and 100 at second 60.
widget.model:
**Three designs.** A fixed window keeps one counter per client per minute and resets it at each boundary. A sliding log keeps each accepted request's time in a deque and counts those in the last minute. A token bucket keeps a token count and a last time. It refills at a steady rate and spends one token per request.

**Accuracy at a boundary.** The limit is 100 a minute. A fixed window admits 100 at second 59 and 100 more at second 60. That is 200 in two seconds. The sliding log admits the first 100 and refuses the rest. All of them are still inside the last minute.

**Memory.** The fixed window stores one number per client. The token bucket stores two. The sliding log stores a time for every accepted request, up to 100 per client. A million clients can then hold 100 million times.

**Bursts.** A bucket of capacity 100 allows a burst of 100 at once. Then it refills at $100/60$ a second, so the average stays bounded. The log never allows more than the limit in any window.

**Choice.** For a hard cap that can be audited, I would use the sliding log and free idle clients. If bursts are fine and memory matters, I would use the token bucket. A fixed window suits only a rough guard, where an error of twice the limit is acceptable.

rubric.text: States the three designs and what each stores
Gives the boundary burst with numbers: 200 against 100
Compares memory per design, including the log's cost per request
Explains the bucket's burst up to capacity and its steady average
Makes a justified choice for a hard-cap gateway

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Mark your answer against the rubric.

explain.text: A fixed window is cheap but admits twice the limit at a boundary. A log is exact but stores every request. A bucket stores two numbers and allows bursts up to its capacity.

items.prose: The limit is 100 requests per minute. A fixed one-minute counter resets at each minute boundary. 100 requests arrive at second 59, and 100 more at second 60.
items.question: How many requests does the fixed counter admit?

widget.label: Requests
widget.accept: 200: 100 in each block. A sliding log admits 100

feedback.correct: 200: each block has its own count of 100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The counter resets at second 60.

byKey.sliding: That is the sliding log's answer. The fixed counter resets at second 60 and admits both groups.

explain.text: Second 59 is in the first minute and second 60 starts the second. Each minute has its own count, so both groups of 100 pass. A sliding log would still see the first 100 at second 60 and refuse the rest.

items.question: Put the steps that touch a key in an LFU cache in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Remove the key from the bucket of its current count
If that bucket is now empty and held the minimum, raise the minimum
Add one to the key's count
Add the key to the end of the bucket for the new count
Add the key to the front of the bucket for the new count
lines.why: Each bucket lists its oldest use first. At the front, this key would be the next victim.

feedback.correct: Leave the old bucket, fix the minimum, count the use, join the new bucket last.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A key must leave its bucket before it joins another.

byKey.d1: You put the newest use first. Each bucket keeps the oldest use at the front.
byKey.left-out: Four steps belong. Only the front insertion is wrong.

explain.text: A touch moves a key up one bucket and puts it last there, as the newest use. The minimum rises only when the emptied bucket held it.

items.question: Which of these are $O(1)$ with a dict of nodes and a doubly linked list? Select all that apply.

options.text: `put` of a new key on a full cache
List every key, most recent first
options.why: You counted the walk as constant. Listing $n$ keys touches $n$ nodes.
Keys are not kept in sorted order, so a median needs a sort or a selection.

feedback.correct: Get, put and delete use a lookup plus a few pointer changes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the steps each one takes.

byKey.list: Listing visits every node, so it is $O(n)$.
byKey.median: Finding a median is $O(n)$ at best here, or $O(n \log n)$ by sorting.

explain.text: A dict lookup, an unlink and a push are each constant. Listing every key or finding a median must look at all $n$ entries, so they are linear or worse.

items.prose: An LFU cache has capacity 2, each value equal to its key. Ties go to the least recently used. Operations: put 1, put 2, get 1, put 3, get 2. Then get 3, put 4, get 1, get 3, get 4.
items.question: What is the sum of the get results? A miss returns -1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a use count for each key and evict the lowest.

byKey.tie: You broke the tie towards the most recent. The tie goes to the least recently used.
byKey.zero: You counted each miss as 0. A miss returns -1.

explain.text: After get 1 key 1 has 2 uses and key 2 has 1, so put 3 evicts key 2. After get 3 keys 1 and 3 both have 2 uses, so put 4 evicts the older, key 1. The gets are 1, -1, 3, -1, 3, 4.

items.prose: A research desk keeps its notes in a small in-memory file system. Every path is absolute, like `/desk/a.txt`, and `/` is the root. No call writes to a folder or makes a folder inside a file. `mkdir(path)` makes every missing folder on the path. `write(path, text)` makes the missing folders above the file, then sets its text, replacing any old text. `read(path)` returns the text, or `None` when no file is there. `ls(path)` returns a folder's names sorted, `[name]` for a file and `[]` for a missing path. `rm(path)` deletes a file, or a folder with everything below it. Removing `/` or a missing path does nothing. `mv(src, dst)` moves a file or a folder, with everything below it, to `dst`. It makes the missing folders above `dst` and returns `True`. It refuses, returning `False` and changing nothing, when `src` is missing or is `/`. It also refuses when `dst` exists or lies inside `src`. `size(path)` is the total length of the text in the files at or below `path`. A missing path has size 0. Every method but `ls` must take time in proportion to the names in its paths. The number of files stored must not matter.
items.question: Design `FileSystem` and any classes it needs, from the stub.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests through `run_fs(ops)`. It calls each method by name and keeps what `read`, `ls`, `mv` and `size` return. Test 10 plays 100,000 random steps and must finish within 5 s.

feedback.correct: Each node carries the size of what lies below it, so every step is one walk down a path.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 moves a file. Its length leaves every folder above `src` and joins every folder above `dst`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 writes the same file three times. The new text replaces the old, so the folders above change by the difference in length.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 removes a folder, then tries `/`. The removed size leaves every folder above it, and `/` itself stays.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 asks for three moves that must be refused. Check every refusal before you make any folder for `dst`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 moves `/a` to `/ab`. Compare the names in the paths, not the strings: `/ab` is not inside `/a`.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 timed out. Adding up a folder's files on every `size` call is too slow; keep a running total on each node.

explain.text: Each node keeps the total length of the files below it, so `size` is one walk down the path. `write`, `rm` and `mv` change that total only on the nodes above the change, one walk per path. A moved folder takes its own totals with it, so nothing below it is touched.
